summary.title: Augmenting Long-term Memory
summary.one_liner: Learn how spaced-repetition flashcards in Anki can turn long-term memory into a deliberate choice, and how to use them to understand dense material such as research papers.
keywords: how to remember what you read
takeaways: Spaced repetition expands review intervals after each correct answer, so long-term retention costs far less review time than fixed weekly flashcard review (the author estimates 4 to 7 minutes per card over 20 years versus over 2 hours).
A rule of thumb: if a fact seems worth about 10 minutes of future time, memorize it; strikingly interesting facts go in regardless.
Using Anki in service of a personal creative project works much better than stockpiling knowledge for some future day.
Repeated skimming passes over a research paper, turning basic facts into cards, builds background that makes a thorough read much easier.
summary.summary: Michael Nielsen's essay is an extended, personal account of using the Anki spaced-repetition program for about two and a half years, with roughly 10,000 cards. He explains how Anki's expanding review intervals make long-term retention efficient, and gives time estimates to support this. He then describes using Anki to learn the Unix command line from a short book and to understand the AlphaGo paper for a magazine article, including repeated passes over the text. The essay also places personal memory systems in a wider history, from Vannevar Bush's memex onward, and argues that memory is central to problem solving and creativity.
